extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of English literature; historians of periodical journalism; editors of literary essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for producing early-18th-century periodical essays in the spirit of the Tatler/Spectator: tone, moral purpose, format, audience engagement, and publishing practices that made those journals successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix serious matters with small diversions
rubrics_metrics.description: After our Serious Matters are over, we shall at the end of every Paper, Present you with a little Diversion, as anything occurs to make the World Merry;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure each issue to include weighty content plus a short light diversion at the end; the diversion keeps readers engaged and provides pleasant relief. Example: Defoe's Review promised 'a little Diversion' at the close of each paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure actions, not persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The Business of this Society is to censure the Actions of Men, not of Parties... They do not design to expose Persons but things;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus criticism on public actions, behaviours, or ideas rather than launching personal attacks. Adopt impersonal satire that targets faults or follies, avoiding defamatory or purely personal invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat vice and villanous actions with severity
rubrics_metrics.description: They resolve to treat Vice, and Villanous Actions, with the utmost Severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be morally serious when condemning clear wrongdoing; allow stern treatment for genuine vice while maintaining the essay's overall temper. Balance severity with fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write short, accessible pieces for limited attention spans
rubrics_metrics.description: many men care but for a little reading at a time... thus we wheedle them in, if it may be allow'd that Expression, to the Knowledge of the World, who rather than take more Pains, would be content with their Ignorance, and search into nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose brief, self-contained essays suitable for readers who prefer quick reads; avoid requiring prolonged attention or dense exposition. Aim to entice casual readers toward broader knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain earnestness with cheerful, unpretending tone
rubrics_metrics.description: restraint of his deep earnestness within the bounds of a cheerful, unpretending influence. Drop by drop it should fall, and its strength lie in its persistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey moral seriousness without pedantry or heaviness: use a genial, modest voice and regular, steady publication rather than passionate exhortation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry and appeals to passion
rubrics_metrics.description: he would affect no pedantry of moralizing, he would appeal to no passions, he would profess himself only 'a Tatler.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of didactic or lecturing tones and overt emotional manipulation. Let persuasion come from reasoned, amiable argument and wit rather than moral grandstanding or sensational appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct wit toward a useful, honourable end
rubrics_metrics.description: wit, if a man had it, unless it be directed to some useful end, is but a wanton, frivolous quality; all that one should value himself upon in this kind is that he had some honourable intention in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humour and cleverness purposefully to instruct, reform, or improve manners; avoid mere wit for its own sake. The author's intent should be seen as honourable and socially beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the people plainly and directly
rubrics_metrics.description: speak his mind... to the people themselves every post-day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write for the general public in plain, direct language rather than for elite patrons; engage ordinary readers and make ideas applicable to everyday life and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graceful kindliness and familiar everyday incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Exquisite grace and true kindliness, here associated with familiar ways and common incidents of everyday life, gave many an honest man fresh sense of the best happiness that lies in common duties honestly performed
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate points with small, relatable scenes from daily life; rely on charm, gentleness, and humane observation rather than abstruse allusion or loftiness to win sympathy and instruct readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose frivolities and small frauds without malice
rubrics_metrics.description: free as Christianity itself from malice--for so both Steele and Addison meant that it should be--in opposing themselves to the frivolities and small frauds on the conscience by which manliness is undermined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize social follies and petty dishonesties firmly but without vindictiveness; moral correction should be delivered with charity, not spite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over garnish
rubrics_metrics.description: they seemed indeed at first to think that what was only the garnish of the former 'Tatlers', was that which recommended them; and not those Substantial Entertainments which they everywhere abound in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize substantial, thoughtful content rather than superficial stylistic tricks. Imitators often fail by copying surface features ('maid', 'night cap', 'spectacles') instead of the underlying substantial amusements and lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require fine and particular manner of thinking and knowledge of the world
rubrics_metrics.description: this sort of writing requires so fine and particular a manner of thinking, with so exact a knowledge of the World, as must make them utterly despair of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should possess keen worldly knowledge and subtle judgement; do not attempt this style without a well-formed understanding of social manners, human nature, and current affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend calm playfulness with political engagement when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: they were blending their calm playfulness with all the clamour of the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating political topics, temper partisan heat with measured, playful tone so as to persuade without inflaming. Adjust the plan/name of the journal to suit the desired degree of political engagement (e.g., 'Guardian' to 'guard people's rights').

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular, frequent publication to build influence
rubrics_metrics.description: the 'Tatlers' were penny papers published three times a week... and the daily 'Spectators' which succeeded them... it was through these, and the daily 'Spectators' which succeeded them, that the people of England really learnt to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish frequently and consistently (daily or multiple times weekly) to establish a habitual readership and sustained cultural influence. Frequency supports persistence of moral influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible pricing and distribution to reach broad readership
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Tatlers' were penny papers published three times a week, and issued also for another halfpenny with a blank half-sheet for transmission by post, when any written scraps of the day's gossip that friend might send to friend could be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep price low and enable easy sharing/transfer (e.g., cheap editions with space for letters) to maximize circulation among merchants, coffee-houses, and ordinary readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exposure by excessive vanity or self-assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: he finally ascribed to the ally he dearly loved, the honours of success... with his usual complete absence of the vanity of self-assertion
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/editors should avoid ostentation about authorship and let the work's usefulness and voice, rather than personal fame-seeking, carry authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allegory and light narrative devices where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a trick of voice common to all, and some papers of Defoe's might have been written for the 'Spectator'. Take the little allegory... which tells of a desponding young Lady... whose name proved to be--Modesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ short allegories, personifications, and illustrative narratives to make moral points vivid and memorable, provided they are tasteful and support the essay's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt journal plan to author's aims
rubrics_metrics.description: He changed the 'Spectator' for the 'Guardian', that was to be, in its plan, more free to guard the people's rights... In place of the 'Guardian', which he had dropped when he felt the plan of that journal unequal to the right and full expression of his mind
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose or revise the periodical's format/name/plan to match the political or moral purpose you intend to pursue; if a plan cannot express the intended voice, change it.
